newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Accused Serb's wife tells of intimidation by Moslems.
newsitem.headline: Accused Serb's wife tells of intimidation by Moslems.

text.p: The wife of an alleged Bosnian Serb murderer and rapist on Wednesday described an atmosphere of intimidation and fear which prompted Serbs to flee the mainly Moslem town of Kozarac in north western Bosnia in early 1992.

Mira Tadic, 35, testifying as a character witness for her husband Dusko "Dule" Tadic, before the U.N. criminal tribunal for former Yugoslavia, said fear of their once friendly Moslem neighbours drove them from their home in the Prijedor region.

Former cafe owner and police officer Tadic, 41, denies charges that he moved at will through Serb-run detention camps in north western Bosnia in 1992, killing, raping and torturing non-Serbs at will as part of a programme of "ethnic cleansing".

Mira Tadic said her husband had been close friends with many in the Moslem community before war broke out in the region in May 1992, describing how Moslems had lent the Tadic family money to set up their cafe, doing some building work for no pay.
But tensions grew in late 1991 and early 1992 as nationalist groupings began to jockey for influence, she said, forcing rifts in the once close-knit community.

"The Serbs wanted to remain in Yugoslavia the way it was at that time. The Moslems wanted their own state, Bosnia, and the Croats wanted a state of their own. Every one was turning to follow their own leaders," she said.

The tensions became more personal as the windows to their cafe were smashed twice, the cafe was burgled and the couple recieved death threats, while Mira, a nurse, faced hostility from her workmates at the Kozarac hospital.
"We got a letter saying that we should leave Kozarac, that if we didn't leave within three months we would be killed. It was signed by the Moslem party -- the SDA," she said.

"At that time in Kozarac it was not safe any more. We were the minority. The Moslem people became organised, they had their barracks, their uniforms, their guns...I was afraid," she said, explaining why the family moved out of Kozarac in April 1992.

When asked by defending lawyer Steven Kay if Tadic spent protracted periods away from the family during the spring and summer of 1992 Mira Tadic replied: "No", adding Tadic spent most nights at home with his family.

Addressing prosecution allegations that Tadic was often to be seen armed and in camouflage uniform after war broke out, Mira Tadic said it had been impossible to move around the region without either of those trappings.

She said Tadic had not been a member of the military when the war broke out and that the assault rifle he possessed had been handed over to him by a deserter from the 1991 conflict in Slovenia to return to the military authorities.
The couple fled Bosnia for Germany in 1993 after a vendetta erupted between them and the local military police chief, who wanted premises they had been promised for a cafe in Prijedor.

Mira Tadic, under cross examination from prosecutor Michael Keegan, said she new nothing official about a bribery investigation against Tadic by the Prijedor police, saying he had been put under pressure by the police for speaking out against police-backed removal of property from Kozarac.

The defendant, arrested in Munich in 1994, is one of seven indicted war crimes suspects held at the tribunal's detention centre. Tadic's trial began in The Hague on May 7 and is expected to end by late November.

The tribunal has indicted 75 suspects, primarily Serbs, but most remain at large, including the two most prominent: deposed Bosnian Serb leader Radovan Karadzic and military commander General Ratko Mladic.
